mappings.note: The MCQ twin of the ethanol short-answer item d018281c, and mapped identically on purpose: both ask whether a combustion that leaves no residue breaks the law. LO-49 is the outcome for exactly that question and the frame gives no basis to separate the two formats.

Four samples reduced to ratios, and the odd one out flagged as a different substance. This applies the law of constant proportions as a test, which is LO-40. Not LO-48, which would cover only naming or stating the law, as sibling 13950474 does.

Name the law from its statement - familiarity level, and LO-48's 'elements combine in fixed ratios form compounds' is the concept being recognised. LO-40 is reserved in this map for items that explain or apply the law rather than identify it.

Reading four shared electrons off a diagram and concluding double covalent bond. The graded content is how the bond is constituted, LO-40's covalent formation clause; the ionic distractor does not make this a differentiation item (LO-39), since no properties are compared.

Recall of the canonical fixed ratio, water 1:8, against three wrong pairings. Concept recognition, LO-48. Its long-answer relatives that compute with the same ratio (1b40a8da, 6880d5a5) go to LO-40 instead.

The reason clause is the definition of a mixture - variable proportions - which is why the law fails there. LO-40 carries the law; C1.2's 'types and properties of mixtures' carries the contrast, and it is the only thing separating this item from the rest of the constant-proportions family.

Conservation of mass explained BY Dalton's indivisible atoms. LO-40 is the only outcome naming Dalton's atomic theory, and this item is exactly the bridge between the theory and the law, which is LO-40's own pairing.
MCQ version of the carbon monoxide 3:4 numerical (f7b241fc). Same outcome, stated openly: the frame has one constant-proportions outcome and no basis for splitting a ratio calculation by item format.
After one electron moves, P is P+ and Q is Q- - LO-41's 'calculate the charge on an ion'. The transfer is depicted rather than explained, so the formation clause of LO-40 is not what is graded.

Hingula/cinnabar is a history-and-culture item: an ancient pigment identified with a modern composition. C5.2 is the frame's only home for science examined through a social-sciences lens, and LO-48 carries the thin chemistry (a compound has a definite elemental composition). Flagged as a weak fit - the question is historical recall and no outcome really wants it.
A four-row property table used to pick out the ionic solid. LO-39's property-based differentiation of ionic and covalent compounds is the exact demand; nothing is formed, named or computed.

Selecting the genuine Dalton postulates, with divisibility planted as the false one. Dalton is named only in LO-40, so every postulate item in this chapter maps there; LO-48's particle clause is a consequence of the theory, not the theory itself.

Substance Z categorised from a conductivity test in two states. Property-based classification of an ionic compound, LO-39 - the sibling item 9d6814a5 asks instead why the solid fails to conduct, and shares the same outcome for the same reason.
Four hypothetical ions with stated valencies, crossed over to test which written formula is right. LO-42's valency-to-formula clause; the valencies are given, so LO-41 is not engaged.

The false statement is that atoms of different elements can share a mass - a direct contradiction of a Dalton postulate. LO-40, the Dalton outcome; the item is about the theory's content, not about telling two species apart (LO-39).

Burning magnesium read through Dalton: atoms rearrange, they are not created or destroyed. LO-40 again, and specifically the postulate that underwrites conservation of mass - the item asks what happens to atoms, not what happens to the balance reading (LO-49).

The distractors are an ion, a crystal lattice and a mixture; the student must pick out what a molecule is against them. That is species differentiation, LO-39's explicit 'atoms and molecules' clause, rather than any formation mechanism.

Why hydrogen and chlorine combine at all: incomplete valence shells drive them to share. LO-40's formation clause. Worth noting that the octet rule itself is named only in competency C1.1's text and in no learning outcome, so items of this shape sit on LO-40 by extension.

Defines a covalent bond by its mechanism - mutual sharing - against an ionic-transfer distractor. LO-40 covers formation of covalent compounds; LO-39 would apply if the item compared the two compound classes' properties, which it does not.

Proton and electron counts for four species, then pick the cation and the anion. Charge on an ion, LO-41. The cation/anion vocabulary also appears in LO-39, but nothing is differentiated by property here - it is an arithmetic comparison of two counts.
Three claims about how HCl forms, with a false transfer step planted. The graded content is the covalent mechanism, LO-40, not the naming (LO-42) or any property (LO-39).

N2O5 to dinitrogen pentoxide by prefix rule - LO-42's 'scientific conventions' clause. This nomenclature block shares LO-42 with the formula-writing block because the frame has no separate naming outcome; the notes are the only place the split is visible.
Why 'mono' is dropped from the first element. A convention rule rather than a name to produce, but still LO-42 - it is the one outcome covering scientific conventions and symbols.

Four formulae matched to four prefix names. LO-42. Considered LO-46 and rejected: a matching exercise is not the design of an educational game, and stretching LO-46 here would be the only way to make that code appear in this chapter.

Ordering the events of O2 formation: unstable atoms, sharing two pairs, octets complete, double bond established. Mechanism, so LO-40. Its part-6 relative 6c6e3007 asks for the same mechanism as a drawing plus explanation and shares the outcome.
